answer:
Judgment: Westpac's targeted FY26 productivity is mainly an offset, not a source of positive jaws. The >$500m target is only about $100m above the $402m of productivity delivered in FY25, and it sits against FY26 cost pressures of a similar order.

The FY25 bridge sets the base. FY24 expenses of $10,944m moved to $11,916m via staff costs +$397m, technology +$146m, volume and other +$199m, productivity -$402m, investments +$359m and a restructuring charge of +$273m. Productivity covered only 37% of the $1,101m of gross pressure. Income rose 3% (from $21,763m to $22,464m) against 9% expense growth, so jaws were about -5.7ppts, or about -3.2ppts excluding the restructuring charge. The cost to income ratio ex Notable Items went from 50.3% to 53.0%.

The FY26 pressures are large. The EBA increase is 3% to 4% on a $6,326m staff expense base, plus a superannuation increase. About 610 announced front line bankers (~350 Business, ~80 WIB, ~180 Consumer) were only c.40% to c.60% onboarded at Sep-25, so a full year cost still arrives. UNITE spend rises to $850m-$950m at ~75% expensed, which is roughly $638m-$713m through the P&L against roughly $488m-$502m in FY25 (our arithmetic on the disclosed 74%-76% expensed share of $660m). Amortisation rose $106m to $995m in FY25 and its FY26 growth is guided only to 'moderate', not to stop.

What actually creates positive jaws in FY26 sits outside productivity. The $273m Fit for Growth charge is 2.3% of the FY25 expense base, so its non-repeat alone lowers FY26 reported expense growth by that amount. The investment mix cuts the other way: total spend stays at ~$2bn with growth & productivity and risk & regulatory both falling, but UNITE is ~75% expensed against 60% for total spend in FY25, so a flat envelope pushes more cost into the P&L.

The UNITE step-up does decelerate. FY25 added $399m of UNITE expense; FY26 adds roughly $140m-$225m on our arithmetic. But UNITE runs at c.40% of a c.$2bn p.a. envelope in FY27-FY28 and the plan extends into FY29, so the drag persists well past FY26.

Conclusion: on this disclosure the productivity target neutralises the run-rate rather than creating headroom. Positive underlying jaws in FY26 require revenue growth above roughly 1% to 2%, and Westpac gives no FY26 revenue guidance.

limitations: Westpac gives no FY26 income or revenue guidance in these documents, so jaws cannot be computed from the disclosure. Only 1H26 NIM sensitivities are given (presentation page 24).
Westpac does not say whether a further restructuring charge occurs in FY26, nor does it disclose the total Fit for Growth program cost, its FTE impact or its benefit profile by year.
'>$500m targeted productivity in FY26' is not defined as gross or net, and Westpac does not state that the FY25 productivity bar of $402m is measured on the same basis.
UNITE cost-out benefits are not quantified anywhere in these documents. No dollar benefit target, payback or timing is disclosed, only qualitative achievements.
The two documents disagree on the FY25 UNITE expensed share: 74% (results announcement page 19) against 76% (presentation page 15).

'c.40% of total investment spend FY27 - FY28' is ambiguous. With its footnote it reads as UNITE being about 40% of a c.$2bn per annum envelope, but it could also mean 40% of the UNITE program total falls in those two years.

The split of UNITE cost between the 'Staff costs' and 'Investments' bars of the FY25 bridge is not disclosed; staff expenses are separately said to include UNITE (results announcement page 18), so the bridge categories are not clean.
The FY26 UNITE expensed step-up of roughly $140m-$225m, and the FY26 expensed investment total, are our arithmetic on disclosed figures, not disclosed numbers.
Segment expense growth rates are distorted by compositional changes and Westpac did not restate FY24 comparatives.
No FY26 FTE, banker hiring or property footprint target is given, so the size of the remaining banker cost to come cannot be quantified.
